beats.narration_text: A CEO hedges every sentence — and one word in the wrong place can flip the whole meaning. I'm Anjana. Here's the one idea, called attention, that lets a model catch it.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Hello, Anjana'; ask types itself
runningText 'reading the sentence twice…'
output lines resolve: 'left-to-right gets it wrong' / 'every word sees every other word' / 'that is all attention is'

props.segment: Attention Is All You Need (To Read an Earnings Call)
props.command: A CEO says 'We expect revenue to remain broadly in line with prior guidance despite near-term headwinds.' An older model reads that left to right and gets the tone wrong. Can you show me what attention actually does differently?
output: every word sees every other word

beats.narration_text: A CEO says "We expect revenue to remain broadly in line with prior guidance despite near-term headwinds." That is twenty words. A human reads it in three seconds. But which word matters most? It depends on which other words are in the sentence. That is attention.

show.event: the full sentence lands center screen as separate neutral-grey word blocks, evenly spaced
a question mark floats above the sentence — on 'which word matters most?'
a soft brightness pulse ripples across all the words simultaneously — on 'That is attention'

beats.narration_text: Older models read left to right. One word at a time, in order. By the time the model reaches "headwinds" at the end, it has already decided how to feel about "revenue" at the beginning. It cannot go back. So a sentence that starts positive and ends cautious gets classified as positive, because the model made up its mind too early.

show.event: same sentence, same word blocks; a glowing cursor starts at 'We' and moves left to right at a steady pace
'revenue', 'broadly in line', 'with prior guidance' turn green as the cursor passes; a verdict bar above fills green, 'POSITIVE', well before the sentence ends
'despite' turns amber, 'near-term headwinds' turns amber/red — but the verdict bar barely moves, already mostly filled
verdict locks in 'POSITIVE ✓' in green, then a red ✗ stamps over it
label lands: 'Left-to-right. Made up its mind too early.'

props.sparkLine: Made up its mind too early.

beats.narration_text: A transformer does not read left to right. It reads everything at once. Every word looks at every other word and asks one question: how much do you matter to me? "Revenue" looks at "headwinds" and increases its attention. "Broadly" looks at "in line" and locks on. "Despite" looks at everything before it and reweighs the whole sentence. This is self-attention. Every word has context from every other word before any decision is made.

show.event: same word blocks reset to neutral; 'revenue' glows, thin lines fan to every other word, two glow thick: 'revenue'↔'headwinds' (spanning the full sentence) and 'revenue'↔'in line'
'despite' glows; thick lines radiate to 'revenue', 'guidance', 'headwinds' — earlier words dim slightly as despite takes influence
all words activate at once — a dense, organic mesh of connections, some thick, some faint, pulsing gently; label: 'Self-attention. Every word sees every word.'
the web funnels upward into a verdict bar that fills amber, 'NEUTRAL / CAUTIOUS', with a green ✓

beats.narration_text: Financial language is built to be ambiguous. CEOs hedge. Lawyers soften. Analysts qualify. A single sentence can start with optimism, pivot on "however," and land on caution, all in twenty words. Without attention, the model reads the optimism and stops. With attention, the model sees that "however" reweighs everything before it. That is why attention changed financial NLP. Not more data. Not bigger models. The ability to see the whole sentence at once and understand that the last word can change the meaning of the first.

show.event: example 1: 'We delivered strong results but expect moderation going forward.' — one thick line 'strong'↔'moderation' through amber-glowing 'but'; split verdict: without-attention 'POSITIVE' (green, wrong ✗) vs with-attention 'CAUTIOUS' (amber, correct ✓)
example 2: 'Margins improved sequentially although headcount reductions contributed significantly.' — line 'improved'↔'reductions' through 'although'; split verdict 'POSITIVE' ✗ vs 'MIXED' ✓

example 3: 'Revenue grew twelve percent excluding the impact of foreign currency fluctuations.' — line 'grew'↔'excluding'; split verdict 'STRONG POSITIVE' ✗ vs 'QUALIFIED POSITIVE' ✓ — resolves fastest of the three

props.sparkLine: The last word can change the first.

beats.narration_text: One idea. Every word sees every other word before any decision is made. That is attention. And it is all you need to read an earnings call.

show.event: the Beat 1 sentence returns with the full attention web from B03 visible, pulsing gently
the web pulses once, brightly — on 'That is attention'
sentence and web dissolve together into the title — on 'all you need to read an earnings call'
title lands: 'Attention Is All You Need' / '(To Read an Earnings Call)'

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Older models read left to right and commit too early. A transformer reads the whole sentence at once — every word attends to every other word before any decision is made. That single mechanism is why a hedge word like "however" or "despite" can flip the meaning of everything before it. Not more data. Not a bigger model. Just attention.

props.artifactHeading: One mechanism. The whole sentence, at once.
artifactLines: Older models read left to right and commit too early.
A transformer reads the whole sentence at once.
Every word attends to every other word before any decision is made.
That is why a late hedge word can flip an early one's meaning.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. "I read a sentence in my own field that has a pivot word in it — a 'but,' an 'although,' an 'excluding,' a 'however' — and I have a habit of reacting to the first half before I finish the second. Can you help me: one, find three sentences from my own recent work where that pattern shows up; two, tell me honestly whether my first read of each one matches what the whole sentence actually says once the pivot word lands; and three, if it does not, name the specific habit I would need to change to stop making up my mind too early?" Paste that into Claude and see whether you have a left-to-right problem of your own.
